Pressure and choking: why easy targets get missed

Choking means shooting clearly below your usual level because of pressure. One common explanation: under pressure you start checking, step by step, a skill that normally runs on its own, and that disrupts it.

Some research

Worry also pulls attention away from the target. In one study of elite shotgun shooters under anxiety, the final look at the target got shorter, the gun moved less smoothly, and they hit fewer targets.

Some research

Signs you can notice on the stand:

  1. Your tempo changes: you rush the call, or stand too long.
  2. You consciously check the gun mount or the swing.
  3. Your eyes go to the barrel or the bead instead of the target.
  4. You keep looking at the scores or at your rivals.
  5. Your grip and shoulders get tighter.
  6. You miss targets that are usually easy for you.

Coaches' experience

What can help: your usual routine and tempo, and one simple cue about the target. A review of 47 studies on choking found that a routine and one simple cue word for the whole shot are among the things that help. More in Pre-shot routine: the same steps in the same order and Cue words and self-talk.

Some research

Process goals keep your mind on what you do rather than on the result: see Process goals and the score.

Some research

Training under mild pressure that grows step by step can prepare you for the real thing. Examples: “five in a row”, a scored practice round, a practice shoot-off, a few spectators, a time limit. More in Training for competition.

Some research

A skill you learned mostly by doing, without many spoken rules about elbows and feet, tends to hold up better under pressure. That is one reason many coaches keep technical talk for training and give only short cue words at competitions.

Some research

In a shoot-off, keep the same routine and the same tempo. Rushing under pressure has been linked with worse results, for example in football penalties.

Some research

Tip: If you may be in a shoot-off, stay warm, drink water and stay close. In both disciplines you may have to shoot within 15 minutes of the call (Chapter 18 · Shoot-off squads, call-up and postponement, Chapter 14 · Staying available for a shoot-off).

Most of this research comes from lab tasks and other sports; the shotgun data come from Olympic trap and skeet. So most likely it works the same way in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting.

If pressure keeps spoiling your competitions over a long time, a sport psychologist can help you build a plan.

Key points

  • Choking often comes from consciously steering a skill that usually runs on its own.
  • Signs: a changed tempo, checking the mount, eyes on the bead, watching the scores.
  • Keep your usual routine, tempo and one simple cue.
  • Train under pressure that grows step by step.
  • In a shoot-off: the same routine and the same tempo.

Did you know?

Some athletes keep a song running in their head during a competition. In one small study, this kind of distraction helped athletes who tended to choke.

For the coach
  • Raise the pressure in training a little at a time, and stop a pressure drill before technique breaks down. Notice which targets fail first under pressure: they show what to train.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Which is a typical sign of choking on the stand?

    1. Your tempo stays just as in training
    2. You start consciously checking your mount
    3. You drink a little water between the stands
    Answer

    You start consciously checking your mount

    Consciously checking a skill that usually runs on its own is a common sign of choking.

  2. What tends to help under pressure?

    1. Changing your technique on the day itself
    2. Checking the scores after each stand
    3. Your usual routine and one simple cue
    Answer

    Your usual routine and one simple cue

    A review of choking studies found that a routine and one simple cue are among the things that help.

  3. How can you shoot a shoot-off?

    1. With your usual routine and tempo
    2. Faster, to get it over with
    3. Slower, checking each movement twice
    Answer

    With your usual routine and tempo

    Rushing and over-checking are both signs of pressure; your usual routine and tempo are a good default.
